Questions.

What is my card worth?

Scan a card and Card AI suggests likely matches from the catalog. Review the set and card number, confirm the finish and language, then choose a raw condition or enter the grade shown on an existing slab to see the relevant market value.

What should I look for in a trading card scanner app?

A useful trading card scanner app should show likely catalog matches for review, keep the set and card number visible, separate raw condition from existing slab grades, and connect confirmed cards to price history and a collection tracker. Card AI does not authenticate cards or predict grades from a photo.

Which trading card games does the card scanner support?

Card AI supports Pokemon, Magic: The Gathering, Yu-Gi-Oh!, One Piece, Disney Lorcana, Digimon, Dragon Ball Super and Naruto cards in one collection, so supported games do not need separate collection apps.

How does Card AI identify a card from a photo?

Point your camera at a card, or select photos from your library. AI recognition suggests matching catalog records with details such as the set and card number. You review the match and confirm fields such as finish and language before adding it.

Can I scan more than one card at a time?

Yes. Bulk scanning lets you work through a stack of cards in one session and add them to your collection together, instead of looking up each card individually.

Does Card AI work with sports cards?

Yes. Alongside supported TCG titles, Card AI covers basketball, football and soccer cards, so you can check their values and track them in the same collection.

Can I track my collection value over time?

Your collection works as a portfolio. Card AI tracks the total value of everything you own, shows price history and market trends for individual cards, and updates as the market moves.

Does Card AI handle graded cards?

Yes. You can record a card as raw with its condition, or as third-party graded with the grading company and grade, covering PSA, BGS, CGC and SGC. Each is tracked and priced separately, so you can compare what the same card is worth raw versus graded.

Do I need to scan a card to look up its price?

No. You can search the card catalog by name, set or card number and open a matching record to see its current market price, price history and details. Scanning is the faster route when the card is in front of you.

h1: Basketball card scanner and value checker.
bodyHtml:
Basketball cards

Basketball card scanner and value checker.

Parallels and rookie cards drive basketball prices. Card AI narrows the catalog so you can confirm the version before pricing it.

DownloadApp Store Store Link PendingGoogle Play

The parallel is the card

Modern basketball releases print the same player image across a long ladder of parallels, many of them serial numbered. The base card and a numbered parallel from the same set are completely different assets, and the numbering is often the only visible difference.

Card AI suggests matching records with the set and card number. In Review, confirm the parallel and finish before using the selected record for pricing.

Rookie cards carry a premium that does not transfer

A player's rookie-year cards trade on a different curve from everything printed afterwards, and that premium is specific to the rookie printings. Recording the set per card keeps rookie and non-rookie copies separate in your collection rather than merged under a player name.

Using a Bowman basketball checklist

Use the publisher's 2025-26 Bowman Basketball checklist spotlight as a starting reference. Check the exact season and product name on the card or packaging. Bowman, Bowman Chrome and Bowman University are not interchangeable product names.

Keep the player, printed card number or prefix, insert and parallel together. A stamped serial number such as /50 identifies the print run of a parallel; it does not replace the collector number in the checklist. Match those details before using a basketball card value or saving a holding.

A broad Bowman result does not prove that a particular checklist entry is covered in Card AI. Search the exact product and player in the app, review the suggested record, and keep an unavailable printing as unavailable. This reference does not promise a complete 2025-26 Bowman catalog or a price for every parallel.

Raw and graded basketball cards tracked apart

  • Raw cards are stored with their condition
  • Graded cards are stored with the grading company and grade, across PSA, BGS, CGC and SGC
  • The same card can be held as both a raw copy and a graded one, each with its own value

You enter the grade from the slab. Card AI does not predict what a raw card would grade.

bodyHtml:
Bulk scanning

Bulk card scanner.

A bulk card scanner app should reduce repeated entry without hiding review. Card AI keeps up to 10 camera or gallery items in one queue before you confirm them.

DownloadApp Store Store Link PendingGoogle Play

The bottleneck is entry, not identification

Looking up a single card is easy and always has been. What defeats people is volume: a few thousand cards, most of them low value, with the ones that matter buried somewhere inside.

A batch card scanner is built for that shape of problem. Add up to 10 camera captures or gallery selections to the current queue, review each suggested match, then continue with the next batch. It does not continuously auto-capture cards or read an entire binder page in one shot.

Find the keepers inside the bulk

Most of a collection is worth very little and a small part carries almost all the value. You cannot tell which is which until everything is identified and priced.

Scanning the whole stack surfaces that split, so the cards worth sleeving, grading or selling stop being invisible.

Everything lands in one collection

Each result enters Review with its matching card record. Confirm the card, choose its finish and language, and set a raw condition or existing slab grade before adding it to your collection. There is no separate spreadsheet or import step to reconcile.

h1: Card AI vs CollX: what does the price represent?
bodyHtml:
Pricing comparison

Card AI vs CollX: what does the price represent?

A scan can identify the right card and still leave a pricing question. Compare how each app records the copy you own and explains the value you see.

DownloadApp Store Store Link PendingGoogle Play

Variant, condition and price are separate decisions

QuestionCard AICollX
Which printing?Suggests catalog candidates for you to confirmIts FAQ says it shows multiple variants for selection and offers manual search
What condition?You choose a raw condition or enter the grade on an existing slabIts FAQ says users manually enter condition or grade; it does not assess condition from a scan
What does the value use?Published market price for the confirmed record and available history; sports cards may link to eBay searchIts FAQ describes marketplace transactions, a median from recent sales, fallback last sale, and an estimate when direct sales are absent
What happens next?Keep distinct holdings in a portfolioAdd to collection; CollX also documents its marketplace

A useful test with two copies of one card

Take one raw copy and one PSA slab of the same printing. In each app, confirm the exact variant, enter the raw condition or slab grade, and note whether the displayed figure is a current estimate, a last sale or a historical trend. This makes an appraisal question concrete. Neither a scanner result nor a marketplace estimate authenticates the card.

CollX is a fit if its built-in buy, sell and trade workflow matters to you. Card AI focuses on reviewed catalog records, condition-specific holdings and collection value. Both products support sports cards; neither should be described as uniquely supporting them.

Read the source of the number

CollX explains its median, fallback and estimate rules in its pricing FAQ. Card AI shows its published market price and available history; an eBay link for sports cards opens a separate search and is not a synced feed of sold transactions. Comparing those figures as if they are the same metric can mislead a seller.

Sources were reviewed October 19, 2026. We have not measured recognition or valuation accuracy on matched physical cards.

Ludex also documents sports and TCG categories. Card AI supports basketball, football and soccer; category breadth alone is not a reason to claim one product is better.

Choose based on selling plans

Do not treat a listing ask as a sold price. Review actual transaction evidence before deciding what to charge.

How to compare the two fairly

Use the same known cards in both apps, including one base card, one parallel, and one graded slab. Record whether each result needs correction, how condition or grade is entered, and what happens after adding it to a collection. h1: Trading card collection tracker.
bodyHtml:
Collection

Trading card collection tracker.

In the Card AI app, save the exact cards you own, see their available prices in one portfolio, and follow price history for each holding.

DownloadApp Store Store Link PendingGoogle Play

A collection becomes useful when it becomes a portfolio

A list can tell you that a card exists in a box. A collection tracker answers the financial question behind that list: what the confirmed holdings are worth together.

Cards enter through scan or catalog search, then contribute their available current price to the portfolio total after you confirm the relevant printing and grading state. That makes the same page a trading card portfolio tracker without turning inventory organization into a second competing owner.

Valuation keeps each holding distinct

  • Each entry is linked to a catalog card with its set and card number
  • Finish and language are confirmed when the entry is added
  • Raw copies carry their condition; graded copies carry the grading company and grade
  • Identical copies can use quantity, while different conditions, finishes, languages or grades remain distinct entries

Price history explains the portfolio movement

A current total is only the latest point. Card AI keeps available price history on individual cards, so you can separate a collection-wide move from one valuable holding changing sharply.

That makes the page a portfolio tracker rather than another catalog view: it is organized around value, contribution, and change over time.

Keep a set checklist separate from your holdings

A checklist shows which numbered cards belong to a set. Your collection records which copies you own, including quantity, finish, language and condition or existing slab grade. A full set's reference value is not the value of your personal holdings.

Use the public Ascended Heroes card list, Chaos Rising card list or Phantasmal Flames card list to check a numbered entry, then add the confirmed copy in the Card AI app. The Pokemon card value guides help separate selected printings before you save them. These public lists do not read your account or mark cards as owned.

Card collection tracker questions.

What should a card collection tracker app keep separate?

It should keep distinct printings, finishes, languages, raw conditions and existing slab grades as distinct holdings. Card AI links each entry to a confirmed catalog record, while the digital card binder handles inventory search and organization.

Can I track duplicates of the same card?

Yes. Copies are stored as separate entries, distinguished by condition, finish, language and grade, so two copies of the same card in different states are tracked and valued independently.

Does the collection value update on its own?

Yes. The total reflects current market prices for the printings you own and moves as those prices change, rather than holding the value from when you added the card.

Can I add cards without scanning them?

Yes. Search the card catalog by name, set or card number and add a matching record directly.

Can I use this as a Pokemon card collection tracker?

Yes. Filter the collection to Pokemon, keep each confirmed printing and condition or grade distinct, and follow the available price history and portfolio value for the cards you own.

Is this a card collection app or a collection manager?

Both descriptions fit. As a card collector app it catalogs what you own; as a collection manager it tracks condition, grade, quantity and value per entry. The distinction matters less than whether the records are tied to real printings, which they are.

How is card collection value calculated?

Each entry is priced on its own printing and condition or grade, and the card collection value is the sum of those. Because entries are tied to real printings, the total moves with the market instead of holding the price from when you added the card.

Does it work as a TCG collector app for a single game?

Yes. The collection filters by game, so it works as a TCG collection app for one supported title or as a single tracker across supported TCG and sports-card categories.

One price for a card is usually the wrong price

Asking what a trading card is worth without saying which copy is like asking what a used car costs. The answer depends on the printing, the condition, and whether it has been graded.

Card AI prices the specific copy. Raw cards are broken out by condition, graded cards by grading company and grade, so a PSA 10 and a lightly played raw copy of the same card never share a number.

Price history matters more than the current price

A single current price tells you what the market thinks today. It does not tell you whether that price has doubled over six months or is sliding after a reprint announcement.

Card AI keeps price history and market trends on individual cards, which is what you need to decide between selling now, holding, or buying more.

Two ways to use the card price scanner

  • Scan the card with your camera, review the suggested catalog matches, and confirm the printing details

How to check Pokemon TCG card prices

A Pokemon card price checker and a Pokemon card value checker answer the same question only after you identify the copy. Start with the set and collector number, then confirm the artwork, finish and language. Choose the raw condition you actually have, or enter the grade already printed on a slab.

From price check to portfolio

Checking one card is useful once. The value compounds when the cards you check become a tracked collection with a running total that updates as the market moves, so you know what the whole thing is worth without re-checking card by card.

Because the card price database sits behind every entry, a card price scanner result and a text lookup resolve to the same number.

Checking a card once answers a question. Watching it answers a better one.

Why the exact printing decides the price

Two Pokemon cards can show the same artwork and the same name and be worth very different amounts. What separates them is the printing: the set, the card number, whether it is a first edition or unlimited run, and whether the card is holo, reverse holo, or non-holo.

Raw and graded Pokemon cards are priced separately

Grading changes what a Pokemon card is worth, sometimes by an order of magnitude. Card AI keeps the two apart instead of averaging them.

bodyHtml:
Blog

What is my trading card worth?

2026-09-22 · Updated 2026-10-19

"What is my card worth" is the most common question in collecting, and the honest answer is that a single card usually has several different prices at once. Knowing which one applies to your copy is the whole skill.

The same card has more than one price

Pull up any well-known card and you will find prices that disagree with each other by a wide margin. That is not the market being broken. It is four variables doing their job:

  • The printing. Set, card number, edition and variant. A first edition and an unlimited print of the same card are different assets.
  • The finish. Holo, reverse holo, foil, borderless or plain. The market prices these separately.
  • The condition. A near-mint raw copy and a lightly played one are not interchangeable.
  • The grade. A graded card trades in a different market from a raw one.

Any tool that gives you one number for a card name is averaging across all of that, which means it is wrong for your specific copy in a way you cannot see.

Start by identifying the exact printing

Before you can price a card you have to know which card you have. The reliable signals are on the card itself: the set symbol, the collector or card number, the edition marking, and whether the surface is holo or foil.

This is the step people skip, and it is the step that produces most bad valuations. A scanner should narrow the catalog to plausible matches with details such as the set and card number. You still need to review that match and confirm the specific finish, language and condition or slab grade before valuing the copy.

Then decide whether you are pricing raw or graded

Once you know the printing, the next fork is grading.

Raw cards

Raw cards are priced by condition. The market generally works in bands, from near mint down through lightly played and worse, and the spread between the top and bottom band on a valuable card can be large. Be honest about condition. Centering, edge wear and surface scratches all count, and a card you think is near mint often is not.

Graded cards

A graded card carries a grade from a third party such as PSA, BGS, CGC or SGC, and it trades on that grade. The jump between adjacent grades is rarely linear. On a sought-after card the gap between a 9 and a 10 can be several multiples, because the population at the top grade is small.

This is why raw and graded prices should never be blended into one figure. They are answering different questions.

Look at the history, not just today's number

A current price is a snapshot. It cannot tell you whether the card has been climbing for six months or is falling after a reprint announcement, and that trend is usually what you actually want to know.

Before you act on a valuation, look at where the price has been. A card that is worth the same today as it was last year is a different proposition from one that got there by halving.

Which Pokemon cards are worth money?

There is no reliable answer based on the Pokemon's name alone. Pokemon card values vary across sets, printings and conditions. Start with the card number and set, then check the finish and language. Price the raw condition you actually have, or use the grade already printed on a slab. Finally, look at the available price history instead of treating one current number as a guaranteed sale price.

The Pokemon TCG 30th Celebration price and set guide shows why this matters: its 30C and 30C-CC records are separate, and its price examples are dated snapshots. The official set checklist can tell you which card to look for; your confirmed copy and market record tell you which value to inspect.

Checking a card with Card AI

Card AI starts by comparing the photo with its catalog and suggesting likely card records with the set and card number. In Review, you confirm the matching card, finish and language, then choose a raw condition or enter the grade shown on an existing slab. Card AI uses that selection to show the relevant market price and price history.

If you do not have the card in hand, you can search the card database by name, set or card number and reach the same record.

One note on scope: Card AI prices cards by the grade you record from the slab. It does not predict what a raw card would grade if you submitted it. Anyone offering that number is estimating, and the estimate is not what the market pays.

h1: Raw vs graded cards, and what grading does to value
bodyHtml:
Blog

Raw vs graded cards, and what grading does to value

2026-09-21 · Updated 2026-11-05

Grading changes what a card is worth. It does not change the card. Understanding why the market pays more for the same cardboard in a slab is the difference between grading profitably and paying fees for nothing.

What grading actually sells

A grading company does two things. It authenticates the card, and it assigns a condition grade on a fixed scale. What collectors are buying in a graded card is the removal of uncertainty.

With a raw card, the buyer is trusting the seller's description and a few photographs. With a graded card, a third party has already made the judgment and sealed it. That certainty is what carries the premium, and it is why the premium is largest on expensive cards, where being wrong about condition costs the most.

The gap between grades is not linear

New collectors often assume grades scale smoothly, that a 9 is worth a bit less than a 10. The market does not work that way.

On a card with strong demand, the step from a 9 to a 10 can be several multiples, while the step from a 7 to an 8 is modest. The reason is population. Top grades are scarce relative to demand, and each grade below the top has progressively less competition for it.

The practical consequence: the value of grading depends almost entirely on whether your card lands at the top of the scale. A card that grades 8 when you hoped for 10 will often not recover the submission cost.

How to price raw versus graded cards

Start with the same card record, then split the question in two. A raw card needs a condition band such as near mint or lightly played. A graded card needs the grading company and the grade printed on the slab. PSA, BGS, CGC and SGC are not interchangeable labels, and a Gem Mint 10 is not a generic premium that can be applied to every raw copy.

When you need more market context, compare the available price history with comparable sales you verify yourself. For supported sports cards, Card AI links to an eBay search. That link does not import sold transactions into the app, and a current listing is not proof that your copy will sell at its asking price.

Which card grading companies can Card AI record?

For an already graded card, Card AI can record PSA, BGS, CGC or SGC and the grade shown on its slab. Keep that copy separate from a raw card, even if both use the same catalog printing. Check whether a grade-specific market price is available for the selected record before using it in a collection estimate.

This is a way to manage cards that have already been graded. Card AI does not submit cards to a grading company, authenticate a slab, or estimate what grade a raw card would receive. For the app workflow, see the graded card tracker.

What does a card centering calculator measure?

A card centering calculator compares the border widths on a photograph, usually as left/right and top/bottom ratios. It describes one aspect of condition. It does not inspect every surface defect, authenticate a card or guarantee the grade assigned by an institution. Consult the PSA grading standards for that company's criteria rather than treating a ratio as a full grade.

Card AI currently records the grade already printed on an existing slab. The current public app does not include a card centering calculator or raw-card grade predictor. Compare the available prices for confirmed holdings in the graded card tracker; a prediction from another tool is not an existing slab grade to record as a fact.

When grading is worth it

Grading has a real cost in fees and turnaround time. A rough filter:

  • Grade it when the card is valuable, the raw copy looks genuinely clean under proper light, and the premium at the top grade is large enough to clear fees several times over.
  • Leave it raw when the card is inexpensive, when the condition is visibly compromised, or when the top-grade premium is thin.
  • Be skeptical of your own assessment. Centering is the most common reason a card that looks perfect comes back below the top grade, and it is the easiest thing to talk yourself out of noticing.

Tracking both in one collection

If you collect seriously you will end up holding both raw and graded copies, sometimes of the same card. They need to be tracked as separate positions, because they have separate prices and behave differently.

Card AI records each copy with its own status. A raw card is stored with its condition. A graded card is stored with the grading company and grade, covering PSA, BGS, CGC and SGC. The same card can appear in your collection more than once, as a raw copy and as a PSA 10, each valued on its own market.

You record the grade from the slab. Card AI currently does not predict what a raw card would grade from a photograph.
